title: November
hookLine: the month of remembering the dead
tomorrow: what if a birthday were a thank-you to God?

cards: Phones keep the dead in strange places: a contact you can't bring yourself to delete, a saved voicemail, a photo that pops up as a memory on a random Tuesday.
In November, some parishes set a book near the altar, and people write in the names of their dead, so they're prayed for at Mass through the month.
All Souls' Day comes right after All Saints, and the whole month leans toward remembering.

teach.h: CAN LOVE STILL HELP THE DEAD?
teach.b: The question underneath: can love still do anything for someone who has died? The Catholic answer is yes.

In the second book of Maccabees, Judas Maccabeus takes up a collection to offer sacrifice for soldiers who had fallen, and the text says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins."

The catechism points to that verse when it teaches prayer for the dead. Catholics believe in purgatory, a final purification before seeing God, and that the living can help through prayer and the Mass.
So the book of the dead is love with somewhere to go. A neighbor tradition answers the same question in its own words.

teach.h: A CHILD WHO PRAYS FOR THEM.
teach.b: In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except three: ongoing charity, knowledge that keeps benefiting people, and a righteous child who prays for them.
Shared ground: the bond doesn't end at the grave, and a prayer from someone who loved them still counts.

One honest difference: Catholic teaching speaks of purgatory and offers the Mass itself for the dead; Islam doesn't teach purgatory, and that hadith speaks of what a person leaves behind continuing to bear fruit.
Two traditions, each in its own words, both keeping a name in prayer.

how: In November, Catholics pray for the dead, especially on All Souls' Day; some parishes keep a book of the dead near the altar, families have Masses offered for their dead, and some visit graves.

games.q: your friend, who isn't religious, lost her grandmother last year. she asks what writing a name in the parish book actually does. what's an honest answer?
o: Catholics believe prayer helps the dead; for anyone, it keeps a loved name spoken.
it guarantees the person reaches heaven by Christmas.
nothing, really; it's just an old family tradition.
games.why: Maccabees calls praying for the dead holy and wholesome. Catholics believe it helps; you can say what they believe without telling her what to believe.

practice: Take paper and a pen and write the names of your dead, one under another: family, friends, anyone whose loss you still carry. Go slowly, and let each name have a moment before the next.
If you pray, you can hold the list and say the Church's old words: eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. If not, just read the names once more.
